after: ## The three branches of the profession
alt: A table comparing solicitors, barristers and chartered legal executives by typical work, who instructs them, rights of audience, how they are organised and their professional body (Law Society; Bar Council and four Inns of Court; CILEx). Only barristers have rights of audience in all courts as standard.
caption: Solicitors advise and prepare; barristers specialise in advocacy; legal executives specialise early.

after: ## The three branches of the profession
alt: Three qualification routes. Solicitors: degree or equivalent, SQE1 and SQE2, two years’ qualifying work experience, and character and suitability. Barristers: degree, vocational Bar course, membership of an Inn of Court, call to the Bar and pupillage. Chartered legal executives: CILEx qualifications with qualifying employment, specialising from the start and needing no degree.
caption: Three routes in; only the legal executive route needs no degree.

alt: The Legal Services Board, created by the Legal Services Act 2007, oversees three front-line regulators: the Solicitors Regulation Authority, the Bar Standards Board and CILEx Regulation. Serious solicitor cases go to the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal; barristers face independent disciplinary tribunals. Clients complain about service to the Legal Ombudsman, and can sue in negligence since Hall v Simons removed advocates’ immunity.
caption: Misconduct goes to the regulators; poor service goes to the Legal Ombudsman.

alt: Judges listed from the top. Superior judges: Justices of the Supreme Court, Lord and Lady Justices of Appeal, and High Court judges. Inferior judges: circuit judges, recorders (part-time), district judges and district judges (magistrates’ courts). The Lord Chief Justice heads the judiciary and the Criminal Division; the Master of the Rolls heads the Civil Division.
caption: Superior judges sit in the senior courts; inferior judges handle most everyday cases.

alt: Three columns. Civil judges manage cases under the Civil Procedure Rules, decide facts and law without a jury and award remedies. Crown Court judges rule on law and evidence, sum up, direct the jury, may direct an acquittal but never a conviction, and sentence. Appeal judges correct errors, interpret statutes and develop precedent. A table shows which civil judges hear small claims, larger County Court cases and complex High Court claims.
caption: Civil judges decide the case; criminal judges guide the jury; appeal judges shape the law.

alt: A building whose roof is judicial independence, held up by five pillars: security of tenure, immunity from suit (Sirros v Moore), independence from the Executive (CRA 2005 s3, the JAC, the Supreme Court), financial security and political neutrality. Its foundation is the reasons for independence: the rule of law, separation of powers, the Article 6 right to a fair hearing and public confidence. The three specification methods are highlighted.
caption: Five methods hold up independence; the rule of law is why it matters.

alt: Independence is freedom from outside pressure; impartiality is the absence of bias in a particular case. The Supreme Court ruled against the government in R (Miller) 2017 (an Act was needed to give notice of EU withdrawal) and R (Miller) 2019 (prorogation unlawful). In Re Pinochet the House of Lords set aside its own decision because of Lord Hoffmann’s links with Amnesty International.
caption: The Miller cases show independence; Pinochet shows impartiality.
